{"id": "80:5/q07", "question": "How should the Prophet allocate attention between the self-sufficient and those seeking guidance?", "turns_on": "The notes frame the practical direction as priority for receptive seekers, honor of the poor, equal warning to all groups, or the limit of responsibility for those who refuse.", "positions": [{"id": "80:5/q07/p1", "position": "Attend to eager, God-fearing seekers rather than pamper indifferent leaders.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī says the Prophet's duty is to teach devoted companions who come eagerly, not to pursue absent leaders; only seekers of reform who fear God merit this attention. The incident redirected time from unlikely-to-reform Quraysh to poor believers. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ describes the opposed pattern of attending to rich scorners without regard to their purification while neglecting the earnest seeker."}, {"id": "80:5/q07/p2", "position": "Keep company with and honor the poor, and avoid love of the wealthy.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUthmān, as reported by al-Sulamī, separately states the commands to accompany and honor the poor and the prohibition of loving the wealthy. Al-Qushayrī says the reproach is on behalf of the poor; Jishumī calls it a rebuke for attending to the wealthy while neglecting the poor. Jishumī and al-Ṭabrisī report that the Prophet subsequently honored Ibn Umm Maktūm, welcomed him as the person over whom his Lord had reproached him, and asked after his needs; al-Ṭabrisī adds that he appointed him deputy in Medina twice."}, {"id": "80:5/q07/p3", "position": "Warn everyone equally, without privileging status or class.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr explicitly lists the eminent and weak, rich and poor, masters and slaves, men and women, adults and children; God guides whom He wills."}, {"id": "80:5/q07/p4", "position": "The Prophet is not accountable for the self-sufficient person's refusal to purify himself.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr says failure to purify is not the Prophet's responsibility. Iṣlāḥī likewise says he need not pamper those who refuse to come and had assumed more than God required in pursuing Quraysh."}]}
{"id": "80:5/q10", "question": "What incident is reported as the occasion for this passage?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "80:5/q10/p1", "position": "Ibn Umm Maktūm came seeking instruction while the Prophet was urging Meccan leaders toward Islam; the Prophet turned away, and the passage was revealed.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan and others, reported by Jishumī, say Ibn Umm Maktūm interrupted the Prophet's effort to convert Meccan leaders, and God rebuked the Prophet after he turned back to them. Al-Ṭabrisī reports that Ibn Umm Maktūm, also named ʿAbd Allāh ibn Shurayḥ ibn Mālik ibn Rabīʿa al-Fihrī, came while the Prophet was urging Quraysh leaders toward Islam. Another report in al-Ṭabrisī says he repeatedly asked to be taught while the Prophet spoke with ʿUtba ibn Rabīʿa, Abū Jahl, al-ʿAbbās, Ubayy, and Umayya ibn Khalaf."}]}
{"id": "80:5/q11", "question": "How did the Prophet treat Ibn Umm Maktūm afterward?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "80:5/q11/p1", "position": "He honored him, greeted him as the man over whom his Lord had reproached him, and asked about his needs; he also appointed him deputy in Medina twice.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan and others, as reported by Jishumī, give the honoring, greeting, and inquiry about his needs. Al-Ṭabrisī reports these acts and adds the two appointments as deputy in Medina."}]}
{"id": "80:5/q12", "question": "What is reported of Ibn Umm Maktūm at al-Qādisiyya?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "80:5/q12/p1", "position": "Anas saw him there in armor, carrying a black banner.", "reasons": "Jishumī and al-Ṭabrisī transmit Anas ibn Mālik's eyewitness report."}]}
{"id": "80:5/q13", "question": "What is said about the Prophet's disclosure of this passage?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "80:5/q13/p1", "position": "If the Prophet had concealed any revelation, he would have concealed this passage.", "reasons": "Jishumī transmits this saying through Ibn Zayd."}]}
{"id": "87:2/q17", "question": "What guidance follows God's creating and fashioning?", "turns_on": "Whether guidance denotes creatures' instinct for nourishment or human religious guidance by signs and proofs.", "positions": [{"id": "87:2/q17/p1", "position": "Creatures have instinctive guidance toward their allotted nourishment.", "reasons": "Study Quran reports this as one meaning of the following guidance."}, {"id": "87:2/q17/p2", "position": "God leads people to religion and knowledge of His unity through signs and proofs.", "reasons": "Study Quran reports this as another meaning of the following guidance."}, {"id": "87:2/q17/p3", "position": "God guides each kind and individual through creation toward its perfection, acts, appointed course, and lifespan.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī describes this as creational guidance and cites 20:50, where God gives each thing its form and then guides it."}]}
{"id": "87:3/q03", "question": "What is God said to guide creatures toward?", "turns_on": "Whether the phrase is unrestricted or names a particular kind of guidance, and whether religious guidance is read as its principal sense.", "positions": [{"id": "87:3/q03/p1", "position": "Every creature is guided toward its allotted function, course, or benefit; particular examples do not limit the verse.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Abū Ḥayyān, Ālūsī, and Elmalılı expressly keep the scope general. Al-Ṭabarī cites lack of evidence for restriction; Elmalılı cites 20:50. Al-Bayḍāwī, al-Biqāʿī, and Bursawī name inclination, inspiration, signs, and revelation. Ibn ʿĀshūr gives speech, craft, grazing, nursing, and bee architecture; al-Biqāʿī says ordainment needs guidance for completeness. Elmalılı includes planetary orbits, attraction, gases, stones, crystals, salt, coal, and cells. Qutb says provision accompanies creatures throughout life; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī cites 15:21, 80:20, and 2:148. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls this creational guidance: God directs each kind and individual toward its created perfection, acts, appointed course, and lifespan, citing 20:50 for God's giving each thing its form and then guiding it."}, {"id": "87:3/q03/p2", "position": "People are shown good and evil, right and error, felicity and misery; livestock are guided to pasture.", "reasons": "Mujāhid's versions vary between assigned misery or happiness and showing moral alternatives. Al-Rāzī connects the latter to perception and the ability to seek benefit and avoid harm, citing 76:3 and 91:7–8. Al-Zajjāj says the person may prove grateful or ungrateful."}, {"id": "87:3/q03/p3", "position": "God directs each person along the felicity or misery already allotted to that person.", "reasons": "Tustarī says God takes charge of the felicitous and leaves the wretched to themselves; al-Wāsiṭī says each group follows its assigned path. These reports describe an outcome, while other Mujāhid reports describe moral alternatives."}, {"id": "87:3/q03/p4", "position": "God directs males and females, especially animals, in how to mate.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī's preferred explanation says each male finds a female of its own species and learns the species-specific manner of mating; ʿAṭāʾ and al-Qurṭubī compare 20:50. Ibn Qutayba calls the direction inspiration. Ibn ʿĀshūr treats reproductive powers as preserving species."}, {"id": "87:3/q03/p5", "position": "The fetus is guided out of the womb at the completion of its allotted term.", "reasons": "Al-Suddī specifies approximately nine months, sometimes shorter or longer. Al-Māwardī also says the child emerges fully formed."}, {"id": "87:3/q03/p6", "position": "Creatures are guided to seek their apportioned livelihood, and animals to their food or pasture.", "reasons": "ʿAṭāʾ and Abū Muslim say every animal receives a fitting provision; al-Zamakhsharī and al-Nasafī add that God teaches its use. Al-Rāzī says God cares for them. Al-Qummī says an initial measure precedes God's guiding whom He wills toward things."}, {"id": "87:3/q03/p7", "position": "People are taught to discover and use the beneficial properties God placed in things.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī gives food, medicine, and poison as examples; al-Qurṭubī includes extraction of useful properties."}, {"id": "87:3/q03/p8", "position": "A newborn is guided to its mother's breast and to suckling.", "reasons": "Tustarī attributes infant sustenance to divine care and distinguishes explanatory guidance from God's taking charge, citing 76:3. Al-Biqāʿī notes the newborn's instinctive opening of its mouth; Iṣlāḥī pairs implanted need with means and capacity."}, {"id": "87:3/q03/p9", "position": "Humans are led to religion, faith, monotheism, and right conduct through reason, signs, revelation, or prophetic invitation.", "reasons": "Abū ʿAlī connects forms and livelihood with knowledge of unity; Jishumī includes lifespans, signs, and completed reason. Al-Rāzī explicitly prefers religious guidance after physical formation and faculties, arguing that prior clauses already cover worldly constitution; he cites 42:52 for invitation. Qatāda distinguishes God's command and approval of obedience from sin. Iṣlāḥī joins moral awareness and prophetic guidance to trials and consequences."}, {"id": "87:3/q03/p10", "position": "God guides sinners to repentance after allotting their sins.", "reasons": "Al-Sulamī reports this formulation; al-Thaʿlabī and Ibn al-Jawzī transmit it among other views."}, {"id": "87:3/q03/p11", "position": "Some are guided to trust God's guarantee quietly instead of striving for their apportioned provisions.", "reasons": "Al-Sulamī contrasts this with the reported view that people are guided to seek their provisions."}, {"id": "87:3/q03/p12", "position": "People are created for recompense and guided to action.", "reasons": "This is al-Māwardī's fifth possibility."}, {"id": "87:3/q03/p13", "position": "People are guided to perceive and use their endowed faculties and capacities.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī

{"id": "87:3/q12", "question": "How does this verse support the call to glorify God and relate to the surrounding sūras?", "turns_on": "Which surrounding passage or theological purpose supplies the connection.", "positions": [{"id": "87:3/q12/p1", "position": "Creation, proportion, determination, and guidance display God's power, wisdom, and worthiness of glorification.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says they answer how the Lord is known and why He merits praise; Abraham's words in 26:78, Moses' reply in 20:49–50, and the first revelation in 96:1–4 use the same proof. The wonders are abundant and observable. Al-Qurṭubī's teacher says the clauses show divine exaltedness. Elmalılı says finite creatures imply the Lord's transcendence and grounds for trust amid disbelievers' schemes."}, {"id": "87:3/q12/p2", "position": "The verse's acts counter the disbelievers' schemes and prepare the Prophet for his mission.", "reasons": "Jishumī connects it with the preceding warning; al-Biqāʿī and Ibn al-Zubayr tie the plot in 86:15 to God's power and wisdom in 87:1–3. Iṣlāḥī says al-Ṭāriq promises only temporary respite and this sūra turns to reassure the Prophet. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the One who shaped him will secure his retention of revelation and ease his law (87:6, 87:8)."}, {"id": "87:3/q12/p3", "position": "The verse parallels other statements that creation is measured and creatures directed.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr cites Moses' 20:50 and the predestination report; Asad links 25:2 and 20:50. Corpus Coranicum links qaddara to 80:19 and hadā to 93:7; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī cites 15:21, 80:20, and 2:148. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī cites 20:50 for God's giving each thing its form and then guiding it, linking it with 87:2–3."}, {"id": "87:3/q12/p4", "position": "The ordered creation described in the verse bears on the sūra's themes of oneness, revelation, and recompense.", "reasons": "Qutb describes the cosmos as a place of praise, the Prophet's preservation and ease, and the message's roots in earlier scriptures; Study Quran says creation is properly formed without flaw and cites 67:3–4."}]}
{"id": "87:3/q18", "question": "How extensive and beneficial is divine guidance?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "87:3/q18/p1", "position": "It extends through religious and worldly human needs and through the beneficial instincts of other creatures.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī says its range in humans, beasts, birds, and other creatures exceeds description. Al-Naḥḥās reports that God guides creatures to their interests. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says creational guidance reaches each kind and each individual through its acts, appointed course, and lifespan."}]}
{"id": "87:6/q10", "question": "What does “you will not forget” encompass?", "turns_on": "Whether the protected object is Qur’anic recitation, its practice, the law and sūras, or every remembered thing.", "positions": [{"id": "87:6/q10/p1", "position": "The Prophet retains the Qur’an God recites to him, so revelation can be conveyed faithfully.", "reasons": "Zajjāj cites 15:9 for divine preservation. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says no verse is irretrievably lost; Ibn ʿĀshūr stresses full delivery as revealed even as the Qur’an grows. Qutb says this removes the burden of guarding every letter and comforts the community. Bayḍāwī, Bursevī and Ālūsī point to exceptional retention despite illiteracy. Ṭabāṭabāʾī specifies no addition, omission or distortion. Ibn ʿAbbās reports an explicit assurance that God would ensure the Qur’an’s retention after the Prophet reviewed it out of fear of forgetting. Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ appeals to 87:6 and 18:24 to argue that God protected the Prophet from forgetting."}, {"id": "87:6/q10/p2", "position": "He does not abandon acting on revelation’s commands and prohibitions, except superseded practice or concessions.", "reasons": "Junayd says acting on commands and prohibitions is meant; Ibn Kaysān praises his answer in Sulamī and Qurṭubī. Māwardī uniquely connects the concession version to forbidding shirk. Al-Ālūsī calls this reading far-fetched."}, {"id": "87:6/q10/p3", "position": "The promise includes every object of forgetting, not only the recited revelation.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī explicitly includes anything else; Bursevī says the exception ranges over the broadest class of objects. Ālūsī reports perfect memory as a distinct view, then rejects it because of early transmitted interpretation and the consequential fāʾ."}, {"id": "87:6/q10/p4", "position": "It guarantees retention of revealed law and sūras while also calling for continued attention and review.", "reasons": "These sources distinguish the verse from 75:16 and explain that neglecting review remains avoidable."}, {"id": "87:6/q10/p5", "position": "It concerns the truth heard by the Prophet.", "reasons": "Bursevī attributes this wording to al-Rāghib."}]}
{"id": "87:6/q11", "question": "What does the exception for what God wills allow?", "turns_on": "Whether the exception identifies an actual removal, ordinary lapse, deferred revelation, limited practice, or a rhetorical assertion of divine will.", "positions": [{"id": "87:6/q11/p1", "position": "God can remove abrogated recitation, often with its ruling, so it is forgotten or no longer practiced.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī explicitly prefers abrogation and withdrawal. Baghawī, Kashshāf, Rāzī and Ibn ʿĀshūr cite 2:106. Rāzī says it ceases to be recited in prayer then leaves memory. Qurṭubī prefers lifting recitation for a benefit, appealing to the normal force of an exception and the written yāʾ. Iṣlāḥī calls the removed directives temporary and says God signals their end."}, {"id": "87:6/q11/p2", "position": "God may cause actual forgetting as He wills, without specifying abrogation.", "reasons": "Qatāda repeatedly states this open exception. Qurṭubī transmits Ibn ʿAbbās through Abū Ṣāliḥ and Qatāda through Saʿīd. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the object of God’s choosing is omitted by normal Arabic usage."}, {"id": "87:6/q11/p3", "position": "The exception is formal or rhetorical; no forgetting is intended or actually occurs.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ compares 11:107 and ordinary oaths that qualify an intended complete gift. Al-Zamakhsharī adopts the empty-exception reading; Rāzī reports al-Kalbī that no forgetting occurred. Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the exception preserves God’s unlimited power though He will not exercise it, citing 11:108. Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ argues from the Prophet's protection against forgetting that nansa'ha means defer or leave, rather than cause him to forget; he also invokes 18:24."}, {"id": "87:6/q11/p4", "position": "It allows a temporary lapse followed by recollection, without permanent loss.", "reasons": "Several cite the prayer omission and Ubayy’s query; Abū Ḥayyān instead cites ʿAbbād’s recitation reminding the Prophet of verses. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it an ordinary human lapse for which God supplies a reminder."}, {"id": "87:6/q11/p5", "position": "Forgetting may establish a practice for the community.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān attributes this to Ibn ʿAbbās and includes it among actual exceptions."}, {"id": "87:6/q11/p6", "position": "God may defer a revelation that Muhammad has not yet recited.", "reasons": "Māwardī attributes this to Ibn ʿĪsā; Qurṭubī reports it among alternatives."}, {"id": "87:6/q11/p7", "position": "Any forgetting is confined to minor etiquette or sunna, not a required ruling.", "reasons": "Rāzī’s reported argument is that loss of an obligatory ruling would damage the law."}, {"id": "87:6/q11/p8", "position": "The exception concerns material outside the duty to convey, which he may forget before conveying.", "reasons": "Qushayrī adds that God knows the secret and the public."}, {"id": "87:6/q11/p9", "position": "The exception reserves an awareness for his praiseworthy station at resurrection.", "reasons": "Qāshānī allows loss of awareness or forgetting now for that later station."}, {"id": "87:6/q11/p10", "position": "It asserts God’s unrestricted will even within a firm promise or enduring law.", "reasons": "Qutb says the Qur’an repeatedly emphasizes this freedom. Ṭabāṭabāʾī stresses God could cause forgetting though He does not. Rāzī reports al-Farrāʾ that preservation is divine favor rather than Muhammad’s own power, citing 17:86 and 39:65."}, {"id": "87:6/q11/p11", "position": "The qualification teaches saying “if God wills” about the future or keeps the Prophet attentive.", "reasons": "Rāzī cites 18:23–24 for the formula and separately reports vigilance over what might be excepted."}]}

{"id": "87:6/q17", "question": "What broader scriptural or literary parallels are noted for this verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "87:6/q17/p1", "position": "The imperative opening followed by a future first-person plural revelation promise parallels 73:2–5.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum also refers readers to 96:1 for qaraʾa."}, {"id": "87:6/q17/p2", "position": "The sūra’s message belongs to a longer account of revelation, afterlife, and earlier scriptures.", "reasons": "Qutb cites 87:18–19; Ibn ʿĀshūr says confirmation of earlier scriptures comforts the Prophet."}, {"id": "87:6/q17/p3", "position": "Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ reads this promise alongside 18:24 to argue that nansa'ha means defer or leave rather than cause the Prophet to forget.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports Saʿd's appeal to both verses for the Prophet's protection from forgetting."}]}
{"id": "92:7/q14", "question": "What occasions or incidents are reported for this promise?", "turns_on": "The narratives identify different acts and people as the setting of the promise; the palm-sale versions also vary in the exchange price.", "positions": [{"id": "92:7/q14/p1", "position": "Abū Bakr freed vulnerable converts despite his father's advice to free strong protectors.", "reasons": "Ibn Isḥāq and ʿĀmir ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr say he sought God's face or reward; Ibn Kathīr locates the freeing in Mecca. Some versions emphasize tortured converts; a Bilāl version names Umayya ibn Khalaf and a garment and ten coins. Another Ibn ʿAbbās route names Abū Sufyān as the opposed miser."}, {"id": "92:7/q14/p2", "position": "A stingy palm owner denied fallen dates to a poor family; Abū al-Daḥdāḥ bought the tree and donated it.", "reasons": "ʿAṭāʾ says the owner refused the Prophet's offer of a Paradise palm. Versions say Abū al-Daḥdāḥ traded an orchard; Ibn ʿAbbās says forty palms. The buyer receives a promised Paradise palm. The contrasting figures' efforts are mapped to verses 5–10. Qurṭubī reports that in this story al-ḥusnā is the reward and the easy way is Paradise."}, {"id": "92:7/q14/p3", "position": "At sunrise two angels pray for replacement of the spender's gift and ruin of the hoarder's wealth.", "reasons": "Māwardī transmits Qatāda through Khulayd from Abū al-Dardāʾ; the Prophet then recites these verses, with no grading stated."}]}
{"id": "92:8/q01", "question": "Who is the miserly, self-sufficient person?", "turns_on": "Whether reported names restrict a general description; al-Alusi objects specifically to Abu Sufyan because of his later Islam.", "positions": [{"id": "92:8/q01/p1", "position": "A general human type; named people are examples rather than limits.", "reasons": "Al-Razi cites 92:4 and 92:14 for the sūra's general scope. Al-Alusi says the wording is general despite reported occasions and treats named people as instances; Kuran Yolu likewise says its message and rulings remain general. Ibn Ashur describes the traits as those of a polytheist; Qutb and Kuran Yolu describe a selfish disbeliever."}, {"id": "92:8/q01/p2", "position": "Umayya and Ubayy, the sons of Khalaf.", "reasons": "Ibn Masud names both; al-Durr's report sets Abu Bakr's purchase and freeing of Bilal against their efforts and identifies al-husna as the testimony of faith and the hard path as Hell."}, {"id": "92:8/q01/p3", "position": "Umayya ibn Khalaf.", "reasons": "Ata and Ibn Abbas name Umayya; other reports contrast him with Abu Bakr, including the account of Bilal's purchase for a garment and ten coins."}, {"id": "92:8/q01/p4", "position": "Abu Sufyan ibn Harb.", "reasons": "Muqatil and al-Kalbi name him, and reports contrast him with Abu Bakr. Al-Alusi questions this identification because Abu Sufyan later became a strong Muslim in Sunni accounts."}, {"id": "92:8/q01/p5", "position": "The Ansari owner of a palm tree.", "reasons": "Ata's account says he refused a palm in Paradise when his tree's dates fell into a poor neighbor's yard; Abu al-Dahdah acquired and gave the tree to the neighbor. Ibn Abbas's version says the believer traded forty palms for it; the owner is set against the giver. Al-Qurtubi identifies the miser in this account as the Ansari."}, {"id": "92:8/q01/p6", "position": "Abu Jahl.", "reasons": "Tustari applies the traits to Abu Jahl; a narration via al-Tusti from Ibn Abbas names him as the occasion."}]}
{"id": "92:8/q08", "question": "What do the contrasting descriptions teach about people's paths?", "turns_on": "Whether the paths describe present moral formation, withdrawal of grace, or their final destinations; Abu Hayyan objects to the grace explanation.", "positions": [{"id": "92:8/q08/p1", "position": "Human striving divides into generous and miserly paths with opposed outcomes.", "reasons": "Razi says deeds culminate in reward or punishment. Ibn Ashur reports the two groups as those enabled to ease and hardship or as the two triads in 5 and 8–9; 99:6–8 illustrates even tiny deeds' outcomes. Qutb calls them two ranks and says each receives facilitation. Islahi says 8–10 describe the character and belief ending in Hell. Bint al-Shati places diverse earthly endeavors under the oath of night, day and creation; Corpus Coranicum says virtue and vice receive eschatological outcomes."}, {"id": "92:8/q08/p2", "position": "The miser's chosen course brings evil deeds and ultimately Hell.", "reasons": "Thalabi and Baghawi say he is turned toward disapproved deeds and punishment, and al-usra may name Hell itself. Qurtubi points to 3:180 for wealth's worldly consequence. Qashani says wealth veils God; Qutb says this rejection brings the greatest corruption. Islahi says God lets worldliness continue smoothly until death and then comes 74:17's steep hardship. Al-Qurtubi glosses the hard way as Hell in this account and al-husna as the reward."}, {"id": "92:8/q08/p3", "position": "God withdraws grace, making obedience especially hard.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan reports Zamakhshari's argument from the constricted heart in 6:125 but rejects its Mu'tazili insinuation."}, {"id": "92:8/q08/p4", "position": "The paths are named for their outcomes or are afterlife roads to Paradise and Hell.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan reports Zamakhshari's alternative explanation of ease and hardship."}]}
{"id": "92:11/q02", "question": "What kind of wealth is meant, and what value can it have at the fall?", "turns_on": "Whether the explanation specifies the hoarded wealth and its missed uses, or states the broader inability of wealth to avert the end.", "positions": [{"id": "92:11/q02/p1", "position": "The wealth he withheld or hoarded cannot rescue him then; benefit belongs to wealth spent rightly and good deeds sent ahead.", "reasons": "Muqātil names Abū Sufyān's hoard. {"id": "92:11/q08", "question": "Which people or event are linked with the revelation of this passage?", "turns_on": "Different attributions name Abū Sufyān, Abū Jahl, the palm owner and Abū al-Daḥdāḥ, or Abū Bakr; the palm report's status as an actual occasion is disputed.", "positions": [{"id": "92:11/q08/p1", "position": "It concerns Abū Sufyān ibn Ḥarb and his withheld wealth.", "reasons": "Muqātil identifies his hoarded money as useless at death and the Fire; Thaʿlabī transmits al-Kalbī's attribution."}, {"id": "92:11/q08/p2", "position": "It concerns Abū Jahl.", "reasons": "Al-Durr transmits Ibn ʿAbbās telling Nāfiʿ b. al-Azraq that the verse concerns Abū Jahl while explaining the fall into Fire."}, {"id": "92:11/q08/p3", "position": "The contrasting figures are Abū al-Daḥdāḥ and the owner of the date palm.", "reasons": "Thaʿlabī reports that a palm dropped dates into a neighbor's yard, its owner refused the Prophet's offer of a palm in Paradise, and Abū al-Daḥdāḥ bought and gave it away. Qurṭubī identifies the owner as an Anṣārī and maps ease to Paradise, hardship to Hell, and death to loss of wealth. Ibn ʿĀshūr reports that a hypocrite took fallen dates from poor Muslim children, Abū al-Daḥdāḥ paid an orchard of forty palms, the Prophet praised his future date clusters, and Bashshār b. Burd alluded to the small palm in verse. Ibn ʿAbbās attributes revelation through al-ʿusrā to the story, but Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the report gharīb and cautions that 'revealed concerning' can mean a verse covers the event rather than that it occasioned revelation. Qurṭubī identifies the palm owner who enters the Fire as a hypocritical Khazrajī who died in hypocrisy; Abū al-Daḥdāḥ is kept from the Fire."}, {"id": "92:11/q08/p4", "position": "Verses 5–19 were said to concern Abū Bakr, while their message remains general.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu reports other interpreters' attribution and stresses that any occasion does not limit the passage's message and rulings."}]}
{"id": "92:16/q04", "question": "Who is the person described by 'the one who denied and turned away'?", "turns_on": "Whether the relative description marks a general class, disobedient refusers, or particular Meccan opponents.", "positions": [{"id": "92:16/q04/p1", "position": "The description identifies an unbeliever or polytheist as the wretched person.", "reasons": "Al-Hasan identifies the most wretched as a polytheist, while Mu'adh adds the phrase 'who denied and turned away.' {"id": "92:16/q10", "question": "What occasion or incident is connected to this warning?", "turns_on": "Whether the reports specify the original occasion or serve as applications of a general early Meccan warning.", "positions": [{"id": "92:16/q10/p1", "position": "The passage concerns Umayya ibn Khalaf and others who denied Muhammad.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas names Umayya and others who denied Muhammad and earlier prophets; the al-Dahhak route adds those like him. {"id": "92:17/q05", "question": "Whom does al-atqā describe?", "turns_on": "Whether reports of an occasion fix the referent and whether the singular definite elative also covers others.", "positions": [{"id": "92:17/q05/p1", "position": "Abu Bakr is its named instance.", "reasons": "Al-Farra, Ibn Abbas, Urwa and many commentators name him; al-Wahidi, Ibn Atiyya, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Razi, and al-Itqan report consensus in their respective circles. Ibn Kathir treats him as foremost under the wording. His freeing of persecuted slaves and selfless spending are cited as fitting traits; al-Razi rejects Ali because prophetic care would count as a favor to repay. Al-Alusi reports sound chains from Ibn Masud and Ibn Abbas."}, {"id": "92:17/q05/p2", "position": "Abu al-Dahdah is its named instance.", "reasons": "Al-Tha'labi ties the designation to giving away the purchased palm solely for God's face; al-Qurtubi gives the same contextual alternative. hat event is reported behind the pious giver?", "turns_on": "Which donation story is transmitted and, within the Bilal story, how he was purchased.", "positions": [{"id": "92:17/q06/p1", "position": "Abu Bakr bought and freed vulnerable people persecuted for faith.", "reasons": "Urwa counts seven, including Bilal, Amir ibn Fuhayra, al-Nahdiyya and daughter, Zunayra, Umm Isa, and a Banu al-Muammal bondwoman. {"id": "92:17/q08", "question": "How do the two apparent restrictions about Hell fit together?", "turns_on": "Whether 'only' yields a logical converse, whether ṣaly means any entry or severe torment, and whether the superlatives mark classes or exemplary figures.", "positions": [{"id": "92:17/q08/p1", "position": "The paired superlatives are rhetorical portraits of exemplary opponents, not strict exclusions of everyone else.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhshari likens the Fire and Garden to places made for the leading disbeliever and believer; examples are Abu Jahl or Umayya and Abu Bakr. Al-Kashf approves. Al-Alusi prefers this after weighing alternatives, though he notes the Mu'tazilite premise about grave sinners. Islahi rejects a literal inference that only the extremes are damned or saved. Al-Qurtubi gives the contrasting figures as a hypocritical Khazrajī who enters the Fire and Abū al-Daḥdāḥ who is kept from it."}, {"id": "92:17/q08/p2", "position": "The earlier ṣaly is exceptionally severe burning, so other sinners may enter or receive lesser punishment.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Munir's lexical report likens ṣaly to placing an animal between layers of coals. Al-Alusi accepts this resolution; al-Baydawi and al-Biqa'i distinguish sinful believers' temporary entry from the wretched unbeliever's abiding fate."}, {"id": "92:17/q08/p3", "position": "Descriptive restriction has no valid converse: less pious people are not thereby condemned.", "reasons": "Al-Razi says al-Qadi himself rejects such implication and that it would wrongly send children and the insane to Hell. Al-Alusi gives this possible reply but finds the earlier 'only the most wretched' harder. Al-Jishumi says children and the insane are outside the warned audience. Islahi says the inference would equally and wrongly restrict salvation to only the most pious."}, {"id": "92:17/q08/p4", "position": "The two elatives name broad classes of wretched unbelievers and pious believers.", "reasons": "Abu Ubayda, quoted by al-Nasafi, and the generic readings use afʿal as an ordinary descriptor. Al-Alusi objects that this alone leaves sinful believers, poor pious people, children and the mentally ill difficult to place."}, {"id": "92:17/q08/p5", "position": "The indefinite 'a Fire' can denote one level of Hell rather than every level.", "reasons": "Al-Qadi proposes this; al-Zamakhshari objects that the following restriction still seems to exclude all but the most pious from that level. Al-Alusi also reports the broader apparent tension."}, {"id": "92:17/q08/p6", "position": "If sinners are not the most pious, the second restriction implies that they enter Hell.", "reasons": "Al-Qadi argues this from the converse. Al-Razi rejects the inference, citing children and the insane and al-Qadi's own view of implication."}, {"id": "92:17/q08/p7", "position": "Only the most wretched enter Hell, so less-wretched people are spared.", "reasons": "Islahi reports this inference; Abu Hurayra's hadith quoted by al-Alusi says only the wretched enter and describes one who neither obeys God nor refrains from sin for God. Al-Nasafi rejects the Murji'ite restriction of entry to unbelievers."}, {"id": "92:17/q08/p8", "position": "At Islam's beginning the contrast matched two actual groups: deniers and fully committed converts.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says the first converts did not commit major sins, so the promise supplies the converse to the warning. {"id": "92:17/q11", "question": "How does the wording connect this verse with the surrounding passage and sura?", "turns_on": "Which surrounding verses or earlier Qur'anic wording the interpreter takes as the link.", "positions": [{"id": "92:17/q11/p1", "position": "It completes the sura's contrast of conduct and recompense for the saved and damned.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shati links the opening oaths over night, day and creation to divergent efforts and final fates. Al-Alusi says the sura details the preceding sura's success and failure. Al-Qurtubi links the miser's wealth failing him at death with the contrasting outcomes: the hypocritical Khazrajī enters the Fire, while Abū al-Daḥdāḥ is kept from it."}, {"id": "92:17/q11/p2", "position": "The phrase parallels 87:11 and recalls taqwā or ittaqā in verse 5.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum gives both the external parallel and the internal word link."}, {"id": "92:17/q11/p3", "position": "The promise that Abu Bakr will be pleased echoes the promise that God's gift satisfies the Prophet.", "reasons": "Al-Biqa'i uses this connection to describe Abu Bakr as closest in the community to the Prophet's station."}]}
{"id": "92:18/q03", "question": "Where or for what is the wealth given?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:18/q03/p1", "position": "It is spent in charity, obedience, and good causes, including help to the poor.", "reasons": "Baydawi, Biqai, and Alusi specify good causes; Nasafi specifies the poor. {"id": "92:18/q12", "question": "What does the giving teach about favors and repayment?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:18/q12/p1", "position": "The giver seeks God's reward without settling a favor owed to anyone.", "reasons": "Razi says repaying a benefactor merely settles a debt; reward follows acting on God's command.
